title: Value Categories, std::move, and Copy Elision
summary: Tell lvalues from rvalues, see that std::move is only a cast, count every copy and move with Tracker, and return big objects for free.
intro: A tick buffer copied by accident costs a fresh allocation and a pass over every tick, on the hot path, with no warning. Whether C++ copies or moves comes down to one property of each expression, its value category. This lesson teaches you to read it, and proves every answer with `Tracker`, a small type that reports each copy and move it goes through.

steps.title: Lvalues, rvalues, and std::move
steps.body:
Whether a line copies a tick buffer or moves it is decided before any of your code runs, by the **value category** of the expression handed over. Every expression has one of three:

| Category | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lvalue | an object with a name or an address, still needed after this line | `t`, `ticks[0]`, `*p` |
| prvalue | a pure value that isn't an object yet | `Tracker{}`, `load()`, `a + b` |
| xvalue | an object you marked as finished with | `std::move(t)` |

Together, prvalues and xvalues are **rvalues**. References bind by category: `T&` takes non-const lvalues, `T&&` takes rvalues, and `const T&` takes anything. That is how `Tracker b = a;` picks the copy constructor and `Tracker c = std::move(a);` picks the move constructor.

`std::move(x)` is only a cast, `static_cast<T&&>(x)`, and it moves nothing. At `-O2`, a function that returns `std::move(t)` for a `Tick& t` and one that returns plain `t` compile to the same two instructions, handing back the address they were given:

```text
as_rvalue(Tick&):
        mov     rax, rdi
        ret
as_lvalue(Tick&):
        mov     rax, rdi
        ret
```

A move happens only if a constructor or assignment taking `T&&` receives the result. Two traps follow:

- `std::move` on a `const` object makes a `const T&&`. A move constructor can't take it, since it must change its source, so the copy constructor runs. Moving a `const` copies, silently.
- A named rvalue reference is an lvalue. Inside `void keep(Tracker&& t)`, `t` has a name, so `Tracker kept = t;` copies. Pass it on with `std::move(t)`.

To prove each answer, this track counts with `Tracker`: every copy or move of one, constructor or assignment, prints `copy` or `move` and adds 1 to `Tracker::copies` or `Tracker::moves`. A moved-from object is still valid but unspecified, as *Copy and Move Semantics* said, so assign it before reading it again.

example.title: Copy, move, or nothing
example.prompt: Initialize and assign Trackers from an lvalue, an xvalue, a prvalue, a const object, and a named rvalue reference, and count what each line does.
example.explanation: `a` is an lvalue, so `b` is a copy. `std::move(a)` is an xvalue, so `c` is a move. `Tracker{}` is a prvalue, which in C++17 builds `d` directly: nothing prints at all. `std::move(b);` on its own line prints nothing either, because a cast does no work. `frozen` is `const`, so its "move" copies. `keep` received an rvalue reference, but inside the function `t` is a name, so `kept` is a copy. Last, `b = std::move(c)` runs move assignment.

practice.title: Make every hand-off a move
practice.prompt:
Every hand-off in the starter copies. Change the code, not the labels, so each one moves.

1. Hand `quote` to `book` with a move: `quote` is never used again.
2. `snapshot` is `const`, which turns its move into a copy. Remove the `const`.
3. In `publish`, `quote` has a name. Move it into `sent`.
4. Move-assign `fresh` into `archive`.

Expected output:

```text
-- hand to the book
move
-- archive a snapshot
move
-- publish
move
-- replace the archive
move
copies 0, moves 4
```

tests.output:
-- hand to the book
move
-- archive a snapshot
move
-- publish
move
-- replace the archive
move
copies 0, moves 4

hints: A `const Tracker` can only be copied, so declare `snapshot` as a plain `Tracker`.
Inside `publish`, write `Tracker sent = std::move(quote);`, and in `main`, `archive = std::move(fresh);`.

steps.title: Where copies hide
steps.body:
In a market-data handler, the copies that hurt are the ones that don't look like copies. A book of price levels, a vector of orders, a buffer of ticks: each line below copies what it touches, and each has a fix.

| Line | What it copies | Without the copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `for (auto lvl : book)` | every element, one per pass | `for (const auto& lvl : book)` |
| `auto best = book[0];` | one element | `const auto& best = book[0];` |
| `[book]() { ... }` | the whole vector, into the lambda | `[&book]`, or `[book = std::move(book)]` to hand it over |
| `auto [px, qty] = level;` | the whole pair or struct | `const auto& [px, qty] = level;` |
| `std::vector<T> v = {a, b};` | each element twice | `reserve`, then `push_back` each |

The last one surprises people. A braced list is a `std::initializer_list`, and its elements are `const`. So the vector must copy them out of the list, even when you write `{std::move(a), std::move(b)}`: that is 2 moves into the list, then 2 copies out of it. Filling a vector without a single copy means `reserve(2)`, then `push_back(std::move(a))` and `push_back(std::move(b))`.

The reference fixes carry the rule from *References and Pass by Reference*: a reference must not outlive what it refers to. `const auto& best = book[0];` dangles once the vector reallocates or dies, so take it, use it, and let it go.

`[book = std::move(book)]` is an init capture. It makes a new member named `book` inside the lambda, initialized from the expression after `=`, so the lambda owns the vector and the outer one is left empty.

example.title: Copies in a level book
example.prompt: Run seven everyday lines over a vector of three Trackers and count the copies each one makes.
example.explanation: `std::vector<Tracker> levels(3)` builds three in place, with no copies. The by-value loop copies each level into `lvl`, three times. The `const auto&` loop and `top` just refer to elements. `auto best = levels[0];` copies one. Capturing `[levels]` copies the whole vector into the lambda, three more, while `[&levels]` stores a reference. The braced list is the expensive line: `std::move(best)` moves into the list and `top` is copied into it, then both are copied out into `two`. That is 1 move and 3 copies for two elements.
example.output:
-- for (auto lvl : levels)
copy
copy
copy
-- for (const auto& lvl : levels)
-- auto best = levels[0];
copy
-- const auto& top = levels[0];
-- [levels] capture
copy
copy
copy
-- [&levels] capture
-- std::vector<Tracker> two = {std::move(best), top};
move
copy
copy
copy
copies 10, moves 1
3 3 2

practice.title: Remove the hidden copies
practice.prompt:
The starter copies 9 times without meaning to. Fix each line so the totals read 0 copies and 2 moves.

1. Loop over `bids` by `const auto&`.
2. Make `best` a `const auto&`.
3. Capture `bids` by reference in `depth`.
4. Build `pair` with no copies: `reserve(2)`, then `push_back` both `x` and `y` with `std::move`.

Expected output:

```text
-- loop
-- best
-- capture
-- pair
move
move
copies 0, moves 2
3 3 2
```

tests.output:
-- loop
-- best
-- capture
-- pair
move
move
copies 0, moves 2
3 3 2

hints: The loop and `best` need only a `&` and a `const`, the same fixes as in the example.
`[&bids]` captures a reference, so the lambda still sees the vector without copying it.
A braced list always copies out of itself. Declare `std::vector<Tracker> pair;`, reserve 2, then `pair.push_back(std::move(x));` and the same for `y`.

steps.title: Returning by value

example.title: Five ways to return
example.prompt: Return a Tracker as a named local, a moved local, one of two locals, a moved member, and a conditional, and count each.
example.explanation: `named` prints nothing: g++ built its local `t` in `r1` itself, with no copy and no move, even at the sandbox's `-O0`. `forced` pays a move only because of its `std::move`. `either` has two locals, so g++ can't build both in `r3`, and it moves the one returned. `s.best` is part of a local, not a local, so a plain `return s.best;` would copy, and `best_of` shows the one place `std::move` in a return helps. `pick` copies: a conditional expression is not a plain name, so even an implicit move doesn't apply.
example.output:
-- named()
-- forced()
move
-- either(true)
move
-- best_of()
move
-- pick(true)
copy
copies 1, moves 3

practice.title: Free returns
practice.prompt:
Make the three return statements as cheap as they can be.

1. In `load_day`, return `day` so that NRVO applies: no copy and no move.
2. In `choose`, replace the conditional with an `if` and two `return` statements, so the result moves instead of copying.
3. In `take_best`, move the member out instead of copying it.

Expected output:

```text
-- load_day()
-- choose(false)
move
-- take_best(Book{})
move
copies 0, moves 2
```

tests.output:
-- load_day()
-- choose(false)
move
-- take_best(Book{})
move
copies 0, moves 2

hints: `return day;` with no `std::move` lets g++ build `day` in the caller's variable.
With `if (use_bid) { return bid; }` and then `return ask;`, each return names a local, so it moves.
`b.best` is a member, not a local, so here `return std::move(b.best);` is right.

steps.title: noexcept moves and vector growth
steps.body:
Quotes and fills pile up in vectors all session. Each time a vector outgrows its capacity, it allocates a buffer twice the size and relocates every element into it. libstdc++ grows 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on, so 1,000 `emplace_back` calls relocate 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512 = 1023 elements in all. As *Copy and Move Semantics* showed, it moves them only if the move constructor is `noexcept`, and otherwise copies. The part that bites in real code is which classes have a `noexcept` move at all:

- A rule-of-zero struct gets an implicit move, and it is `noexcept` when every member's move is. `std::string`, `std::vector`, and `Tracker` all qualify.
- Declaring a destructor, even an empty `~Quote() {}` added for logging, removes the implicit move. There is then no move constructor at all, so every rvalue, `std::move` included, goes to the copy constructor, and growth deep-copies every string.
- `= default` brings the moves back, `noexcept` when the members' are: `Quote(Quote&&) = default;`. Declaring a move deletes the implicit copies, so default those too, the rule of five.
- `std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>` from `<type_traits>` tells you which one the vector will see.

The real fix for a hot path is not to grow during the session at all. `reserve(n)` before the market opens means zero relocations, whatever the moves cost.

example.title: Quotes that grow
example.prompt: Grow vectors of a rule-of-zero quote and of a quote with its own destructor, then reserve first, and count the relocations.
example.explanation: Four `emplace_back` calls grow the capacity from 1 to 2 to 4, relocating 1 element and then 2: three relocations. `Quote` writes none of the five, so its implicit move is `noexcept` and the vector moves. `LoggedQuote` differs only by an empty destructor, yet it has no move constructor at all, its trait is `false`, and the same growth copies the string and the `Tracker` of every element. With `reserve(4)` first, nothing is ever relocated, so even `LoggedQuote` costs nothing.
example.output:
true false
-- Quote, growing
move
move
move
copies 0, moves 3
-- LoggedQuote, growing
copy
copy
copy
copies 3, moves 0
-- LoggedQuote, reserved
copies 0, moves 0

practice.title: A fill log without copies
practice.prompt:
Make a growing fill log move instead of copy, then make it never relocate.

1. Keep `Fill`'s destructor, and bring its moves back with `= default`: default the default constructor, both copy operations, and both move operations.
2. In `fill_log`, call `reserve(n)` first when `reserve_first` is true.
3. The starter reads `n` and runs the log twice, growing and reserved. Leave `main` as it is.

Input:

```text
5
```

Expected output:

```text
true
-- growing
move
move
move
move
move
move
move
copies 0, moves 7
-- reserved
copies 0, moves 0
```

tests.output:
true
-- growing
move
move
move
move
move
move
move
copies 0, moves 7
-- reserved
copies 0, moves 0

true
-- growing
move
move

-- reserved

hints: Declaring any constructor removes the implicit default constructor, which `emplace_back()` needs, so start with `Fill() = default;`. Then the copy constructor, move constructor, copy assignment, and move assignment, each `= default`.
A defaulted move is `noexcept` here because `std::string` and `Tracker` move without throwing, so the trait prints `true`.

recap:
- Every expression is an lvalue (has a name, still needed), a prvalue (a pure value, not yet an object), or an xvalue (`std::move(x)`). Prvalues and xvalues are rvalues.
- `T&&` binds rvalues, `const T&` binds anything. That choice is what picks the move or the copy.
- `std::move` is only a cast. Moving a `const` object copies, and a named `T&&` parameter is an lvalue that copies unless you `std::move` it again.
- `Tracker` prints `copy` or `move` for every copy or move, constructor or assignment, and totals them in `Tracker::copies` and `Tracker::moves`.
- Hidden copies: `for (auto x : v)`, `auto x = v[i]`, a `[v]` capture, `auto [a, b] = s`, and any braced list, whose `const` elements are always copied out.
- `return T{};` is guaranteed elision. `return local;` is NRVO on g++, else an implicit move. Members and conditionals copy.
- Never `return std::move(local);`: it costs a move and blocks NRVO. `return std::move(s.member);` is right.
- A growing vector moves elements only through a `noexcept` move. Declaring a destructor removes the implicit move, so growth copies. `= default` the five to get it back.
- `reserve(n)` before the hot path means zero relocations.

Next, **Passing Data: References, Sinks, and Perfect Forwarding** puts those counts to work on function parameters, and moves a tick buffer through a pipeline with zero copies.
